## Learning Locomotion with MSMs

*Train a policy using reinforcement learning to output muscle activations that achieve high-level locomotion skills, like walking, incline-walking, running, etcetera.*

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.box}
[**Motion Imitation** [@simos2025imitation; @park2025magnet; @cotton2025kintwin]]{style="display:block; text-align:center"}

- Tracks pre-recorded mocap trajectories (motion-mimicking reward).
- Reproduces reference kinematics well.
- Can allow physiologically implausible internal solutions; brittle outside the demonstrations.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.box}
[**Predictive Simulation** [@schumacher2025natural; @badie2025bioinspired; @weng2021natural]]{style="display:block; text-align:center"}
There are two main approaches:

1. Utilize bio-plausible objectives (effort, stability, pain).
2. Build bio-inspired curricula (balance, walk, run).
:::
:::
:::::

Neither approach connects kinematic accuracy with neuromuscular authenticity

- Human-like $\neq$ physiologically plausible: the underlying neuromuscular coordination and joint kinetics are underdetermined.

::: {.notes}
Most of the recent progress has come from motion imitation — the policy tracks a mocap clip using motion-mimicking rewards. That works well for reproducing the reference kinematics.

But the paper's point is that imitation only constrains the surface-level motion. The muscle coordination and joint kinetics underneath are left underdetermined, so the policy can land on internal solutions that aren't physiologically plausible, which makes it hard to use the model to explain anything causally. And since these policies are optimized around the demonstrations, they can be brittle when the speed, slope, or task changes.

Predictive simulation drops the imitation reward. The paper groups it into two strategies: shaping behavior with biologically plausible objectives, like Schumacher et al., and bio-inspired curricula, like Badie and Weng. These have made progress, but matching human joint kinetics and muscle patterns across speeds and slopes is still hard. The paper calls this the gap between visually plausible motion and experimentally grounded biomechanics.
:::
